newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian feed barley prices slide on output - CWB.
newsitem.headline: Canadian feed barley prices slide on output - CWB.

text.p: Better coarse grain production prospects in North America, Europe and Australia led to a C$7 a tonne decline in the Canadian Wheat Board's feed barley price forecast on Thursday, a CWB spokeswoman said.

"The European Union's barley production should be 53 million tonnes and they've increased their restitution (subsidy), the U.S. corn's escaped the frost and Australia's got a larger barley crop," CWB spokeswoman Deanna Allen said.
The International Grains Council (IGC) Thursday increased its world coarse grains output estimate for 1996 by 6.0 million tonnes to 875 million from its earlier forecast.
U.S. coarse grain output, boosted largely by the end of frost concerns for corn, was expected to reach 260.4 million tonnes, up from last month's estimate of 255.6 million tonnes.
The Canadian coarse grain production forecast was raised to 28.5 million tonnes from 27.5 million tonnes, largely on increased barley output.
Australia's barley output estimate rose 1.1 million tonnes to 9.6 million tonnes from September's IGC estimate.
The return of the EU's feed barley export subsidy three weeks ago at 24.99 Ecus which reached 31.09 Ecus (C$53-54 a tonne) this week also weighed on prices, Allen said.
European barley was valued at US$138 a tonne FOB.
The CWB's revised world price forecast for October feed barley prices was C$143-163 (US$106-121) a tonne, FOB St. Lawrence River or Vancouver.

The bottom of the range is now within C$6 of the federally guaranteed CWB initial payment to farmers. The government guaranteed the CWB's initial, or partial downpayment, for No1 Canada Western Feed Barley at C$137 a tonne on July 29.
The initial payment usually reflects 70 to 80 percent of expected returns from world market sales. If world prices fall below that, the Canadian government must still pay that price.
The rise in the Canadian dollar to C$1.3440 Friday from C$1.3733 since the start of the CWB's new marketing year August 1 was another factor weighing on prices, Allen said.
"The stronger dollar's a factor because we trade in U.S. dollars," Allen said.
A stronger Canadian dollar makes Canada grain more costly.

The CWB held an 11 percent share of the world feed barley market in 1994/95 (Aug/July) on exports of 3.84 million tonnes. The United States was its largest customer, buying 1.26 million tonnes, followed by Japan at 968,000 tonnes, China at 384,000 tonnes and Saudi Arabia at 130,000.
